paper_title: PointWAM: 3D World Action Modeling for Dexterous Robotic Manipulation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: World action models jointly learn to forecast world dynamics and predict robot actions, such that the learned internal world dynamics guide accurate actions. Existing approaches typically represent the world as RGB frames or latent counterparts while predicting actions as end-effector poses or joint angles, but they often struggle to capture the 3D spatial structure and contact geometry central to dexterous manipulation. We introduce Point World Action Model (PointWAM), a 3D world action model that decomposes the world into a scene (i.e., environment) and hands (i.e., actor), and jointly forecasts both as 3D point trajectories within a shared space-time coordinate frame. This explicit, disentangled representation enables effective pre-training on large-scale human demonstration videos without requiring any task-specific object or keypoint selection. Given a colored point cloud and a language instruction, PointWAM predicts how the scene and hands co-evolve in 3D space over time, then retargets the forecast hand motion to robot actions. Pre-training on human videos improves average DexJoCo success by 56.9 percentage points, and scene-trajectory supervision adds 10.9 points over forecasting the hands alone. With both, PointWAM surpasses the prior state of the art on ten DexJoCo tasks by 11.7 points and outperforms strong VLAs on a real robot.

Conventional Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) (Black et al., 2025; NVIDIA et al., 2025) map observations to motor commands without explicitly forecasting how the scene evolves. World Action Models (WAMs) have recently emerged as promising alternative by treating world and action modeling as deeply intertwined: they jointly learn to forecast how the world will change and what actions cause those changes (Li et al., 2025a). Many existing WAMs build on video generation backbones and represent the world as RGB frames (Du et al., 2023) or their latent counterparts (Li et al., 2025a; Liao et al., 2026). These representations are limited in their ability to capture key aspects of physical interaction, including 3D spatial structure and causal relations between the actor and the environment. Point-based policies (Haldar & Pinto, 2025; Kim et al., 2026a) address the 3D action prediction problem by forecasting trajectories of 3D points, but do not model how the environment evolves. They also rely on humans or external perception models to select task-relevant objects for their scene inputs. Conversely, action-conditioned 3D world models forecast dense 3D scene trajectories, yet treat robot actions as inputs rather than quantities to be predicted (Huang et al., 2026). In this work, we introduce Point World Action Model (PointWAM), 3D world action model that decomposes the world into scene (i.e., environment) and hands (i.e., actor), and represents both as three-dimensional point trajectories within shared space-time coordinate frame  (Fig. 1)  . This explicit, disentangled world representation enables effective learning of cause-and-effect relations between the environment and the actor by modeling how their points co-evolve in 3D space over time. Given colored point cloud and language instruction, PointWAM forecasts trajectories for every observed scene point and hand keypoint in common coordinate frame. Its action retargeter then converts the forecast hand trajectories into the corresponding robot actions. The proposed approach offers three additional advantages. First, modeling both the scene and hands in shared 3D space enables effective pre-training on human demonstration videos from EgoDex (Hoque et al., 2026) and VITRA (Li et al., 2026b). Second, no task-specific objects or scene keypoints need to be selected in advance, so scene forecasting is not restricted to predefined set of target objects. Third, by decoupling hand-point trajectories from the scene, the forecast hand motion is amenable to effective retargeting onto robot hands for action prediction. Our main contributions can be summarized as follows. We introduce PointWAM, which jointly forecasts the 3D trajectories of scene points and hand keypoints in shared space-time coordinate frame, unifying world and action modeling. We demonstrate that 3D world modeling benefits dexterous manipulation. Scene-trajectory supervision improves average DexJoCo success by 10.9 percentage points over the same model without it, and our 3D encoder outperforms lifted image features by 5.4 percentage points. We show that pre-training on human demonstrations from EgoDex and VITRA improves average DexJoCo success by 56.9 percentage points over training from scratch. With this pre-training, PointWAM surpasses the prior best multi-task success rate on DexJoCo by 11.7 percentage points and outperforms robot-pre-trained VLAs on real robot by up to 25 percentage points.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: We discuss the closest work here and provide broader review in Appendix A. World action models (WAMs). WAMs unify predictive world modeling with action prediction; unlike conventional VLAs, which map visual observation straight to motor command, WAM is trained to forecast how the world will change and predict what actions the robot must perform (Du et al., 2023; Hu et al., 2025; Liao et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2026d; Li et al., 2025a). Existing WAMs typically forecast future visual representations in the latent space of pretrained video models while predicting robot actions as end-effector poses. These models must therefore learn how changes in latent visual features correspond to robot motion, rather than explicitly modeling both scene and hand motion as 3D trajectories. Closest to ours, EgoWAM (Li et al., 2026a), PointWorld (Huang et al., 2026), and PointZero (Duisterhof et al., 2026) forecast dense 3D scene motion. sections.title: 3.4 LEARNING FROM HUMAN AND ROBOT DEMONSTRATIONS
sections.content: We train the trajectory forecaster on human and robot demonstrations and the action retargeter on robot demonstrations alone, since only they record the end-effector poses and finger joint commands that the action retargeter learns to predict (Fig. 1, left). Human demonstrations. Human demonstration videos lack recorded states, so we estimate both trajectories from the videos themselves. Hand trajectories come from the 3D hand poses annotated in EgoDex (Hoque et al., 2026) and reconstructed by VITRA (Li et al., 2026b), mapped to the robot hands ten keypoints. Scene trajectories come from dense 2D point tracks of CoTracker3 (Karaev et al., 2025), lifted to 3D with monocular depth from VGGT-Ω (Wang et al., 2026b) scaled to the annotated hands. The resulting 1.15M episodes share the trajectory format of the robot demonstrations, so both supervise the same forecaster; Appendix B.1 details the preprocessing. Robot demonstrations. Recorded robot states give hand trajectories through forward kinematics. Scene trajectories come from replaying DexJoCo (Wang et al., 2026a) demonstrations, which move each initial point with its object or rigid part, and on the real robot from CoTracker3 (Karaev et al., 2025) tracks lifted with Fast-FoundationStereo (Wen et al., 2026) depth. We process the RoboDojoPrecision demonstrations similarly to DexJoCo (Appendix B.2). Training. We first pre-train the backbone and both trajectory heads from scratch on human demonstrations using scene and hand trajectory supervision. sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: In this section, we describe the experimental setup (Section 4.1) and answer three questions. (1) Does PointWAM, pre-trained only on human demonstrations, outperform policies pre-trained on robot or video corpora in dexterous and high-precision manipulation? (Section 4.2) (2) Does human-demonstration pre-training transfer to robot control, and does it scale with the number of human demonstrations and with model size? (Section 4.3) (3) Does 3D world modeling enable more precise dexterous manipulation than 2D world modeling or model without it, and does 3D encoder help beyond lifted 2D features? (Section 4.4) 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP We pre-train PointWAM on 1.15M human demonstration episodes from EgoDex (Hoque et al., 2026) and VITRA (Li et al., 2026b), which provide scene and hand trajectories but no robot actions, and fine-tune it on the robot demonstrations of each benchmark and of the real robot. 4.1.1 BENCHMARKS AND PROTOCOLS DexJoCo. DexJoCo (Wang et al., 2026a) is simulated benchmark of eleven dexterous tasks, six single-arm and five bimanual, on Franka Panda arms with 16-DoF Allegro hands. Its tasks require tool use, such as driving nail with hammer, and coordination of two hands. We use its objectplacement setting, where no policy reported with the benchmark exceeds 5.3% success on bimanual assembly. We exclude bimanual unlock iPad, since 42 of its 100 demonstrations fail when replayed in the released environment; 959 of the other 1,000 demonstrations pass the replay check. We train one policy across the ten tasks  (Table 1)  and one per task. Each task has one fixed instruction, which tells the multi-task policy which task to perform. Following the official protocol, we run 50 closedloop episodes per task on each of three evaluation seeds and report the success rate (SR) averaged

Appendix C.2 details the protocol, and Appendix reports the results of the single-task policies. RoboDojo-Precision. Although PointWAM is designed for dexterous hands, its point-trajectory representation is not tied to one embodiment. We therefore test whether it transfers to paralleljaw grippers, using the Precision tasks of RoboDojo (Chen et al., 2026b), which hinge on precise placement. Two ARX X5 arms perform these eight tasks, such as inserting key and fastening screws, and each task comes with 100 RGBD demonstrations. We train and evaluate every method on these tasks alone. The tasks are hard; on the benchmark leaderboard, policies trained on all of its tasks rarely complete them (Chen et al., 2026b). We therefore also report its partial-progress score, which separates methods when success is rare. Appendices B.2 and C.3 detail the setup. Real robot. To evaluate PointWAMs manipulation performance in the real world, we use an OpenArm humanoid with two 7-DoF arms, two 6-DoF Inspire RH56F1 hands, and ZED 2i stereo camera, as shown in Fig. 5a. We evaluate two tasks: banana pick-and-place (PnP) and square-peg insertion. Banana PnP evaluates general manipulation ability using single arm, while square-peg insertion evaluates coordinated dexterous manipulation with both hands. We collect 54 demonstrations for banana PnP and 64 for square-peg insertion, and evaluate each method over 24 trials per task. For banana PnP, half of the trials use the banana seen in the demonstrations (in-domain), and the other half use an unseen box whose color resembles the table (out-of-domain). For square-peg insertion, we also report progress score, the mean number of completed stages per trial out of three, lifting each of the two parts and inserting the peg. 4.1.2 BASELINES We take two baselines from DexJoCo (Wang et al., 2026a) with their published results. With one policy across the ten tasks, PointWAM achieves the highest success rate on eight tasks and reaches 69.0% average SR  (Table 1)  , outperforming the strongest baseline, GR00T N1.6, by large margin of 11.7 percentage points, and π0.5 by 19.0. Both pre-train on large-scale robot demonstrations and web data, whereas PointWAM uses no robot demonstrations beyond DexJoCo. PointWAM also ranks first with one policy per task, and its margin over the strongest baseline widens from 5.3 to 22.2 percentage points under full randomization of camera pose, lighting, and texture (Tables 5 and 6 in Appendix D). Figure 3 shows the scene and hand trajectories PointWAM predicts, and Fig. 4 shows bimanual hanoi rollouts from one initial state, where PointWAM succeeds and GR00T N1.6 times out; Appendix shows more rollouts. RoboDojo-Precision. With no robot data beyond the benchmarks own demonstrations, PointWAM reaches an average score of 8.8 and 4.8% SR  (Table 2)  . Fast-WAM and PointACT also pre-train on no robot data, only on videos, image-text pairs, or 3D scenes, and stay near zero (0.3, 0.2% and 1.6, 0.0%), even though PointACT observes depth. GR00T N1.6, whose pre-training includes large-scale robot data with grippers, reaches 6.2 and 2.3%, still below PointWAM, and leads on three of the eight tasks. PointWAM, pre-trained on human hands alone, thus shows initial transfer to grippers, and depth alone does not account for its lead over Fast-WAM and PointACT. Real robot. Figure 5b summarizes the real-robot results. PointWAM outperforms both GR00T N1.6 and π0.5 over all trials of each task. On banana PnP, it performs comparably with the in-domain banana but reaches 58.3% SR with the out-of-domain unseen box, against 16.7% and 25.0%. Since the box resembles the table in color, the RGB-based baselines likely struggle to find it, while PointWAM can rely on its 3D shape. On square-peg insertion, PointWAM reaches 50.0% SR against 16.7% and 25.0%. All three methods usually lift both parts, but the baselines often fail at the insertion, which needs precise bimanual placement; PointWAM inserts in 12 of 21 such trials, against 4 of 19 and 6 of 18. Figure 12 in Appendix shows example rollouts.

We first measure how much EgoDex (Hoque et al., 2026) pre-training improves each method (Fig. 6; whiskers show 1 standard deviation over three seeds), fixing Volt-H and 60k fine-tuning iterations for PointWAM. The baselines already build on large pre-trained models; GR00T N1.6 inherits vision-language and robot-policy pretraining (NVIDIA et al., 2025), and Fast-WAM and PointACT build on pre-trained Wan2.2 (Team Wan et al., 2025) video and Qwen2.5-VL (Bai et al., 2025) backbones (Yuan et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026a). PointWAM instead trains its backbone from scratch, keeping only its frozen encoders pre-trained, and hence starts from lower SR than the baselines. PointWAM nevertheless benefits far more from EgoDex pre-training. Its SR rises nearly fivefold, from 12.1% to 60.1%, whereas the baselines change by at most 1.4 percentage points (GR00T N1.6 from 57.3% to 56.6%, Fast-WAM from 52.9% to 54.3%, and PointACT from 33.7% to 33.9%). Even Fast-WAM, which also forecasts the future but as video frames, gains little. These results suggest that the gain comes from the shared 3D representation, in which human and robot demonstrations take the same scene and hand point trajectories, rather than from world modeling alone. Data scaling. SR rises from 60.1% with EgoDex alone to 64.9% with 736K episodes and 69.0% with the full 1.15M episodes. EgoDex alone already surpasses GR00T N1.6 (57.3%), and the full corpus adds 8.9 percentage points. Model scaling. sections.title: 4.4 COMPONENT ANALYSIS
sections.content: We change one setting at time from common reference, Volt-L12 backbone, named for halving the depth of Volt-L to 12 layers, pre-trained on EgoDex and fine-tuned for 60k iterations  (Table 3)  . Since the ablations require many training runs, the reference is smaller and uses fewer human demonstration videos than the benchmark model, so its SR is lower than in Table 1. Appendix gives the training settings, and Appendix D.2 further varies the patch size and encoder fine-tuning. Vision encoder (a). The 3D encoder Mosaic3D, which computes features on the point cloud, reaches 64.4%. Lifting DINOv3 (Simeoni et al., 2026) image features onto the points, as in PointWorld (Huang et al., 2026), lowers SR to 59.0%. Lifted features carry 3D positions but are computed from images. The gap suggests that encoding the 3D structure of the scene in the features themselves, not only in their positions, matters for dexterous manipulation. World modeling (b). Removing scene-trajectory supervision from both pre-training and finetuning, with the depth input, 3D backbone, and hand head unchanged, lowers SR from 64.4% to 53.5%. Forecasting the scene thus improves success beyond observing it in 3D, and Fig. 3 shows the predicted scene moving with the hands. The 2D frame row uses the DINOv3 encoder of (a) and forecasts the DINOv3 latents of the frame at t+T through learnable queries that read the backbones output tokens, as in FLARE (Zheng et al., 2025) but with DINOv3 rather than SigLIP-2 latents, so that its input and its target share one feature space. It reaches 60.1%, 6.6 percentage points above the model without world modeling but 4.3 below the reference. Forecasting the 3D trajectories of scene points from 3D features thus outperforms forecasting future image latents from image features. Hand representation and voxel size (cd). In (c), anatomical keypoints reach 64.4%, whereas depth-sampled hand surface points reach 43.6% with 10 points per hand and 44.6% with 512. Keypoints likely help because they correspond between human and robot hands (Section 3.1). In (d), 1 cm voxels reach 64.4%, above both finer 0.5 cm voxels (59.9%) and coarser 2 cm voxels (52.2%). Coarser voxels may blur the contact geometry, while finer ones add little detail beyond the 224224 depth input. We therefore use 1 cm voxels in all experiments, including Table 1.

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We have introduced PointWAM, 3D world action model that decomposes the world into scene and hands. It jointly forecasts both as 3D point trajectories in shared space-time coordinate frame and retargets the forecast hand motion to robot actions. Since human videos provide the same trajectories, PointWAM pre-trains on them without selecting task-specific points, raising average DexJoCo success from 12.1% to 69.0% and surpassing the strongest baseline by 11.7 percentage points. Observing the scene in 3D per se is not enough; forecasting the scene adds 10.9 percentage points over forecasting the hands alone. These results suggest that shared 3D point-trajectory representation lets robots learn dexterous manipulation largely from human videos. Since PointWAM sees the world only through points, it can miss details finer than the point spacing, such as printed text, and surfaces that depth sensing cannot capture, such as transparent objects. Future work could extend what each point carries, from finer appearance to physical properties such as mass and friction, which govern how objects move under contact.

sections.title: A EXTENDED RELATED WORK
sections.content: In this section, we extend Section 2 to further world action models, 3D representations for robot policies, and other ways of learning from human demonstration videos. Future targets of world action models. Beyond the dense 3D scene motion forecast by EgoWAM and PointWorld, world action models differ in what future they forecast and what they condition it on. Several forecast geometric futures, such as object poses in DyWA (Lyu et al., 2025) and depth in GAM (Han et al., 2026). 3D-VLA (Zhen et al., 2024) forecasts goal RGBD images or point clouds, and WSA1 (Jiang et al., 2026) forecasts latent 3D scene states. Others keep an image future. Fast-WAM (Yuan et al., 2026) and Cosmos 3 (NVIDIA et al., 2026) build on video generation backbones, 4D-WAM (Yang et al., 2026) aligns its features with 3D trajectory fields during training, and FLARE (Zheng et al., 2025) aligns future tokens of its policy with image features of future frame. X-WAM (Guo et al., 2026) forecasts multi-view RGB-D video alongside actions. In each of these, the forecast future takes different form from the motion that produces the action, whereas PointWAM expresses the scene and the hands with the same 3D point trajectories and retargets only the hands to actions. Dexterous World Model (Kim et al., 2026b) conditions its interaction video on given hand trajectories, much as PointWorld conditions on future robot trajectories, so it also requires supplied hand trajectory rather than forecasting one itself for robot control. 3D representations for robot policies. PointWAM observes the scene as point cloud, which gives policy direct access to 3D geometry. DexPoint (Qin et al., 2022a) and DexArt (Bao et al., 2023) combine observed geometry with kinematics-derived point clouds for dexterous reinforcement learning, and DP3 (Ze et al., 2024) learns imitation policies from encoded point clouds. Even the image-based SpatialVLA (Qu et al., 2025) augments its features with 3D positions from estimated depth. In all of these, geometry serves only as input, and the control objective alone trains the backbone. CordViP (Fu et al., 2025) adds contact and handarm correspondence objectives. PointACT (Chen et al., 2026a) keeps 2D visionlanguage backbone and admits pre-trained 3D point features only in its action expert, through multi-scale pointaction attention, so geometry conditions the action but never the backbones representation. PointWAM also builds on pre-trained 3D features but supervises the backbone with future hand and scene trajectories, which human demonstration videos supply without recorded robot actions. Other ways of learning from human demonstration videos. Beyond the point-based policies in Section 2, methods differ in what they transfer from the video to the robot. Retargeting the human hand pose (Qin et al., 2022b) transfers actions directly but sets no scene-forecasting objective, and neither do the hand and object poses of FlowHOI (Zeng et al., 2026). DexWM (Goswami et al., 2026) learns latent world model from egocentric human videos with hand keypoints as actions, so it forecasts the effect of given hand motion rather than the motion itself, and HarmoHOI (Dang et al., 2026) co-generates handobject interaction videos and 3D point tracks for synthesis rather than robot control. Track-based methods (Wen et al., 2024; Bharadhwaj et al., 2024) forecast the future image positions of arbitrary points, but the tracks and the features behind them stay in image space. General Flow (Yuan et al., 2024) forecasts 3D flow only at query points sampled on the manipulated object, MolmoMotion (Zhang et al., 2026) forecasts 3D trajectories of query points on an object of interest, and µ0 (Lee et al., 2026) forecasts 3D traces of interaction keypoints selected with vision-language model. In all three, something outside the model decides which scene points it supervises. PointWAM instead encodes the full point cloud and supervises the trajectory of every observed point and of the hand, learned from human demonstration videos without robot actions.

sections.content: B.1 HUMAN-DEMONSTRATION PREPROCESSING Human videos record neither robot states nor simulator states, so we estimate hand and scene trajectories from the videos themselves. EgoDex (Hoque et al., 2026) annotates an SE(3) transform for each of 25 joints per hand, and VITRA (Li et al., 2026b) reconstructs 21 joints for each visible hand. We keep the joint positions and map them to the hand keypoints described below. When hand is missing, we mark its keypoints invalid instead of imputing them. Hand keypoints. We turn each human hand into the same ten keypoints as the robot hand (Appendix B.2). Human demonstrations are first rotated, with their scenes, into z-up frame like the robot-base frame of robot demonstrations. At each time t, we build palm frame (ot, Bt) on the human hand, with its origin at the middle knuckle and its axes along the wrist-to-knuckle direction, along the knuckle row, and their cross product. Indexing the ten keypoints of one hand by k, the six palm keypoints overlay the robot palm on the human palm, placing the Allegro palm points at their fixed offsets d(k) from the robots palm in this frame. The four fingertip keypoints are the tracked tips (k) of the thumb, index, middle, and ring fingers: q(k) = ot + Bt d(k) (k = 1, . . . , 6), = (k) q(k) (k = 7, . . . , 10). (8) The little finger is omitted because the Allegro hand has no counterpart to it. Clips. We split each episode into 1 clips of 11 frames at 10 Hz that start every 0.5 s, and discard clips whose summed wrist displacement is below 2 cm. We linearly resample each clip to 31 frames, so that its future steps match the horizon = 30 of the DexJoCo demonstrations. EgoDex contributes 5.2M clips from 324K episodes, and VITRA contributes 824,157 shorter episodes. Depth. VGGT-Ω (Wang et al., 2026b) predicts per-frame depth only up to scale. We recover the metric scale from the hands, which ARKit annotates in EgoDex and VITRA reconstructs. For each chunk of frames, we project the hand joints into the images, discard depth ratios zGT/zpred more than factor of two from their median, and take the median of the remaining ratios as the scale. Scene tracks. We resize frames to 640 360, place queries on every second pixel of each clips first frame, and track them with CoTracker3 (Karaev et al., 2025) in offline mode. Backward tracking is unnecessary, since every query starts at the first frame. Each track reads the scaled depth at its pixels and is lifted to the world frame with the camera intrinsics and poses. We keep points that are visible with valid depth in the first frame, deduplicate them on 1.5 cm grid, and subsample at most 12,000. Since queries restart in every clip, point correspondence holds only within clip. B.2 ROBOT-DEMONSTRATION PREPROCESSING Point cloud and scene trajectories. In DexJoCo, robot fine-tuning and evaluation use 224 224 depth images, which we unproject with the camera calibration, reduce to one point per 1 cm voxel, and crop to box around the robot base, 1 to each side and from 0.2 below to 1 above it. The box adapts the bounds filter of PointWorld (Huang et al., 2026), cube about the scene center, to exclude the floor and walls. Since the DexJoCo dataset records object poses only at reset, we replay each demonstration to recover them over time. For each successful replay, simulator segmentation removes robot points from the initial point cloud and assigns every remaining point, background included, to an object or rigid part, whose rigid motion defines the points trajectory. Robot hand keypoints. Each robot hand has ten keypoints, six on the palm and four on the fingertips. The fingertip keypoints lie on the contact pads, since points on the distal joint axes would miss the motion of four finger joints during flexion. Separate kinematic chains compute the right and left hands, which record their joints in different orders, and each hands measured pose places its keypoints in the scene frame without mirroring one hand onto the other. Bimanual inputs list the right hand before the left and give each hand its own ID. RoboDojo-Precision. Its two ARX X5 arms carry parallel-jaw grippers, so we keep the pre-trained interface and change only what the embodiment requires. Following Point Policy (Haldar & Pinto, 2025), which places robot points by rigid transform about the gripper pose, each arm again has ten keypoints, the six palm offsets placed on the gripper frame from forward kinematics and the two fingertips, with the last point repeated to fill the ten slots. sections.title: C EXPERIMENTAL DETAILS
sections.content: C.1 TRAINING SETTINGS Main model. Table 4 lists the settings of the Volt-H multi-task model in Table 1. We pre-train it for 60k iterations on EgoDex and VITRA (1,148,324 episodes in total) and fine-tune it for 60k iterations on DexJoCo, with the 3D and text encoders frozen in both stages. Component ablations. Ablations use Volt-L12, backbone with width 1024, 12 layers, and 16 heads, which trains 175M parameters. We pre-train it on EgoDex for 40k iterations and fine-tune it for 60k, starting from the pre-training snapshot with the lowest held-out hand-trajectory error (35k for the reference). Every variant, surface points included, changes both pre-training and fine-tuning.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Model scaling. The model-scaling study varies backbone width and depth while keeping the other components fixed. The Volt-S, Volt-B, Volt-L, and Volt-H configurations in Fig. 8 have widths of 384, 768, 1024, and 1280 and depths of 12, 12, 24, and 32. All share frozen encoders with 592M parameters, and during fine-tuning they train 39M, 106M, 326M, and 655M parameters, including the 4.6M-parameter retargeter. Table 1 uses the largest configuration, Volt-H. C.2 DEXJOCO EVALUATION PROTOCOL Inference timing. DexJoCos evaluator runs asynchronously. It requests new chunk once fewer than 24 of the 30 actions remain and holds the robots pose whenever the buffer empties, so inference latency affects the executed behavior. On one B200 GPU, the Volt-L12 reference of Table 3 takes 55 ms per forward pass, 37 ms of it in the frozen encoder. Each simulator control step spans 20 ms, so 30-step chunk covers 0.6 s. Human clips carry the same 31 frames over 1 (Appendix B.1), so one predicted step spans about 33 ms in pre-training and 20 ms in fine-tuning. Checkpoint selection. For the Volt-H multi-task model, we consider the 20k, 40k, and 60k finetuning snapshots and select on the first seeds ten-task average, which selects 60k; all component ablations use 60k. Single-task policies are trained with the view augmentation of Appendix for 20k iterations (30k for bimanual hanoi and microwave) and evaluated at that final snapshot. C.3 ROBODOJO-PRECISION EVALUATION PROTOCOL We use the official RoboDojo evaluator (Chen et al., 2026b). Unlike the DexJoCo evaluator, it runs synchronously. The simulator waits for each query, executes the whole action chunk, and then queries again, so inference latency does not affect the outcome. The evaluation seed selects fixed set of initial layouts, and we run 50 episodes per task on seed 0, taking the layouts in order. An episode ends at success or at task-specific step limit, from 300 steps for insert key and deposit coin to 1,900 steps for fasten screws, that is, 12 to 76 at the benchmarks 25 Hz. We report the success rate and the benchmarks partial-progress score, each averaged over the eight tasks with equal weight. PointWAM is fine-tuned once from the 60k pre-training checkpoint, and we evaluate its 60k fine-tuning snapshot without further selection. The published benchmark instead trains three seeds per policy and evaluates each for 50 trials; we use one training seed and one evaluation seed for every method in Table 2. We leave out the public leaderboard entries, since they are trained on all RoboDojo tasks rather than the Precision demonstrations alone. C.4 REAL-WORLD EXPERIMENTS DETAILS Banana PnP. This task evaluates basic single-arm pick-and-place and, more importantly, the ability to rely on geometry when color cues are ambiguous. We collect 54 demonstrations in which the robot picks up banana from various positions on the table and places it in basket at fixed location. We run 24 evaluation trials per method with positions sampled from those in the demonstrations, 12 with the banana and 12 with box unseen in the demonstrations whose color closely matches the tabletop. trial succeeds if the object lies entirely inside the basket at the end of the episode. Square-peg insertion. This task evaluates precise grasping and tight bimanual coordination: the robot must lift square peg and blue hole, align them, and insert the peg into the hole. Because the peg is slippery, an imprecise grasp allows it to tilt between the fingers, which causes the insertion to fail. We collect 64 demonstrations with the peg and hole placed at various positions, and run 24 evaluation trials per method with positions sampled from those in the demonstrations. Since one end of the hole is capped, trial is successful only if the peg remains in the hole at the end of the episode. To capture partial progress, we additionally score each trial on scale from 0 to 3: 0: fails to lift the peg. 1: lifts the peg but fails to lift the hole. 2: lifts both objects but fails to insert the peg. 3: inserts the peg, which remains in the hole until the end of the episode (success).

sections.content: C.5 BASELINES C.5.1 GR00T N1.6 Following the official recipe,1 we fine-tune from the released GR00T N1.6-3B checkpoint (GEAR Team, 2025). We use the AdamW optimizer with learning rate of 1 104, an action horizon of 30, and input images at 224 224, with all remaining hyperparameters left at their defaults. With global batch size of 256, we train separate model per task for 30K steps (single-arm) or 60K steps (bimanual) in the DexJoCo single-task setting, and single model across tasks for 60K steps in each of the DexJoCo multi-task and RoboDojo settings. For evaluation, we follow the default protocols of DexJoCo and RoboDojo-Precision. For the EgoDex (Hoque et al., 2026) pre-training experiment in Fig. 6, we follow H-RDT (Bi et al., 2026) and convert the ARKit hand annotations of EgoDex into 44-D bimanual state per frame, consisting of the 3D position and quaternion orientation of each wrist, which serves as the end-effector pose, and the 3D positions of the five fingertips of each hand. Since human demonstrations carry no commanded actions, we define the action at step as the next state, so that the model directly regresses future hand states. We pre-train for 30K steps with global batch size of 192, the same budget as for the other baselines. C.5.2 FAST-WAM We use the official codebase2 with the pre-trained Wan2.2-5B model. We train for 100K steps with cosine learning-rate schedule initialized at 1 104, an action horizon of 32, and global batch size of 64. For DexJoCo, we concatenate three 224 224 camera views, while for RoboDojo-Precision, we concatenate three 192 256 views. For evaluation, we follow the default protocols of DexJoCo and RoboDojo-Precision. In Fig. 6, we pretrain Fast-WAM on EgoDex with the same hand-state actions and budget as for GR00T N1.6, with single-view 224 224 videos as visual supervision. C.5.3 POINTACT Following the official implementation3, we initialize the VLM backbone from Qwen2.5-VL-3BInstruct (Bai et al., 2025) and keep it frozen, initialize the point encoder from the pretrained Concerto (Zhang et al., 2025) PTv3-Large (Wu et al., 2024) checkpoint, and train the remaining modules from scratch. We use the AdamW optimizer with learning rate of 5 105 and cosine learning rate schedule, with random rotations of the point cloud about the gravity axis and image augmentations as in the official implementation. With global batch size of 256, we train separate model per task for 30K steps in the DexJoCo single-task setting, and single model across tasks for 60K steps in each of the DexJoCo multi-task and RoboDojo settings. Depth maps for both benchmarks are obtained in the same manner as for PointWAM. In Fig. 6, we pretrain PointACT on EgoDex with the same hand-state actions and budget as for GR00T N1.6.
